stem: Best guess: a client's income will be much higher next year because of a large bonus. Generally, what should she do with deductible expenses she controls?

choices.text: Pay them this year, as early as possible
choices.explanation: Deductions are worth more in the higher-rate year.

choices.text: It makes no difference when they're paid
choices.explanation: The marginal rate differs between years.

choices.text: Delay them to next year's higher rate
choices.explanation: Correct. A deduction saves tax at the marginal rate, so it is worth more in the higher-rate year.

explanation: A deduction saves tax at the marginal rate, so it is worth more in the higher-rate year.

stem: Prior-year AGI was $120,000 and prior-year tax was $18,000. Current-year tax will be $30,000. What is the required annual payment to avoid a penalty?

choices.explanation: 90% of current-year tax is larger than the prior-year safe harbor.
The safe harbors allow less than 100% of current tax.
110% applies only when prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000.

explanation: AGI of $120,000 uses the 100% prior-year safe harbor: lesser of $27,000 or $18,000.

stem: Bunching itemized deductions produces the most benefit when a taxpayer's annual itemized deductions are:

choices.explanation: Correct. Bunching lets the taxpayer itemize in one year and take the standard deduction in the other.

choices.text: Far above the standard deduction every year
choices.explanation: They already itemize every year; bunching adds little.

choices.text: Made up only of state income taxes
choices.explanation: SALT timing is limited by the cap and payment rules.

explanation: Bunching lets the taxpayer itemize in one year and take the standard deduction in the other.

stem: Kim's 2024 AGI was $180,000 and her 2024 tax was $30,000. Her 2025 tax will be $50,000. What required annual payment avoids the underpayment penalty for 2025?

choices.explanation: The prior-year safe harbor is lower.

explanation: High-income taxpayers use 110% of prior-year tax.

stem: A taxpayer owes $900 when filing after withholding. What underpayment penalty applies?

choices.text: None; the balance due is under $1,000
choices.explanation: Correct. §6654(e)(1): no penalty if tax due after withholding is less than $1,000.
That's the failure-to-pay rate, which applies only if the balance isn't paid by the due date.

explanation: §6654(e)(1): no penalty if tax due after withholding is less than $1,000.

stem: A self-employed client earned most of his 2025 income in December. Which method most likely reduces his estimated-tax penalty?

choices.explanation: An extension doesn't extend payment deadlines.

choices.text: Paying the full balance due on January 15
choices.explanation: Earlier installments would still be short under the regular method.
Correct. The annualized method matches required installments to when income was actually earned.

explanation: The annualized method matches required installments to when income was actually earned.

stem: Single taxpayer: wages $180,000, dividends $30,000, and long-term capital gains $20,000. What is the NIIT?
Which income is **not** net investment income for the 3.8% NIIT?

choices.text: Rent from a passive rental property

choices.explanation: Correct. Qualified retirement plan and IRA distributions are excluded from NII.

explanation: Qualified retirement plan and IRA distributions are excluded from NII.

stem: A married couple filing jointly has wages of $150,000 (spouse A) and $160,000 (spouse B). How much additional Medicare tax do they owe?

choices.explanation: Combined wages exceed the MFJ threshold.

explanation: MFJ threshold is $250,000 of combined wages; neither employer withholds (each is under $200,000), so it's paid with the return.

stem: For 2025 the kiddie-tax threshold is $2,700. A 15-year-old has $6,000 of interest income and no earned income in 2025. How much of it is taxed at the parents' rate?

choices.explanation: The first $2,700 isn't taxed at the parents' rate.
The kiddie tax applies to children under 19.

explanation: 2025 kiddie tax threshold: $2,700 ($1,350 standard deduction + $1,350 at the child's rate).

stem: In 2025, a client age 74 must take a $40,000 RMD and plans to give $40,000 to charity. She takes the standard deduction. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Take the RMD in cash and donate it
choices.explanation: Increases AGI; no deduction benefit because she doesn't itemize.

choices.text: Have the IRA pay the charity directly (a QCD)
choices.explanation: Correct. A QCD satisfies the RMD and is excluded from income — better than a deduction she can't use.

choices.text: Skip the RMD and donate from savings
choices.explanation: Missing an RMD triggers an excise tax.

choices.text: Convert the IRA to a Roth IRA first
choices.explanation: Conversion is taxable and doesn't satisfy the RMD.

explanation: A QCD satisfies the RMD and is excluded from income — better than a deduction she can't use.

stem: A single taxpayer expects to move from the 24% bracket in 2025 to the 35% bracket in 2026. Which action most likely reduces total tax over the two years?

choices.text: Accelerate a deductible charitable gift into 2025

choices.explanation: Correct. When rates will rise, pull income into the lower-rate year and push deductions into the higher-rate year.
Gain rates may rise with income.
Converting at the lower rate is better.

explanation: When rates will rise, pull income into the lower-rate year and push deductions into the higher-rate year.

stem: In 2025, a married couple filing jointly with MAGI of $300,000 pays $45,000 of state income and property taxes. What is their SALT itemized deduction?

choices.explanation: Correct. MAGI is under $500,000, so the full $40,000 cap applies.

explanation: P.L. 119-21 raised the SALT cap to $40,000 for 2025, reduced only when MAGI exceeds $500,000.
reviewNote: Uses a One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) amount or effective date for 2025. Verify against current IRS guidance and exam materials.

stem: Which strategy lets a taxpayer claim a large charitable deduction now while recommending grants to charities over several years?

choices.explanation: A QCD isn't a deduction and goes straight to a charity.
Correct. A donor-advised fund contribution is deductible when made; grants can be recommended later.

explanation: A donor-advised fund contribution is deductible when made; grants can be recommended later.

stem: A client's will leaves everything to her children, but her IRA beneficiary designation still names her former spouse. She dies. Who receives the IRA?

choices.explanation: Correct. Beneficiary designations control retirement accounts and override the will.
The will does not govern assets that pass by beneficiary designation.
A named beneficiary receives the account outside probate.
The designation, not a compromise, controls.

explanation: Review beneficiary designations after life events; they pass outside probate and override the will (subject to any state revocation-on-divorce statute).

stem: Which risk can an investor reduce by holding a diversified portfolio?

choices.explanation: Interest rate changes affect the whole market; diversification does not remove systematic risk.
Correct. Diversification reduces unsystematic risk; systematic (market) risk remains.
A recession affects nearly all securities.

explanation: Diversification reduces unsystematic risk only.

stem: A client wants to harvest a loss on an S&P 500 index fund in December but stay invested in the market. Which action achieves both?

choices.text: Buy a fund on another index
choices.explanation: Correct. It isn't substantially identical, so no wash sale.

choices.text: Rebuy the same fund in 2 weeks
Buy the same fund in her IRA
Sell and rebuy it the same day

explanation: §1091 disallows a loss if substantially identical securities are bought within 30 days before or after the sale, including in the taxpayer's IRA.

stem: A client plans to give $50,000 to her church. She owns stock held 5 years (basis $10,000; FMV $50,000). Which approach is most tax-efficient?

choices.text: Sell the stock and donate the cash
choices.explanation: She'd pay tax on the gain.
Correct. She deducts FMV and avoids the $40,000 gain.

choices.text: Donate cash and keep the stock
Donate it after a year-end sale

explanation: Gifts of long-term appreciated stock to a public charity give an FMV deduction (subject to 30% of AGI) and avoid capital gains tax.

stem: A client has an unusually low-income year after leaving her job. Which planning step may be worthwhile?

choices.explanation: Correct. Conversion income is taxed at low rates.
The low year is the opportunity.

explanation: A low-income year can be used to convert traditional IRA money to a Roth at low marginal rates.

stem: A client has room in the 0% capital gains bracket. What can she do with appreciated stock?

choices.text: Hold it to avoid any tax
Gift it to a high earner

explanation: Gains realized within the 0% bracket aren't taxed, and the wash sale rule doesn't apply to gains.

stem: Why is an HSA sometimes called a triple-tax-advantaged account?

choices.text: It avoids estate and gift tax
Tax benefits in, during and out
choices.explanation: Correct. All three stages are favored.

choices.text: It's exempt from state tax everywhere

explanation: HSA contributions are deductible, earnings grow tax-free, and qualified medical withdrawals are tax-free.

stem: A parent wants to shift $10,000 of investment income to her 12-year-old. What limits the benefit?

choices.explanation: Correct. Unearned income is taxed at parents' rates.

explanation: The kiddie tax taxes a child's unearned income above a threshold at the parents' rates.

stem: A client wants to give her grandson stock worth less than her basis. What should she do instead?

choices.explanation: Correct. A gift would waste the loss.
The grandson can't use her loss.

choices.text: Give it to a charity instead

explanation: Built-in losses don't transfer to a donee for loss purposes, so selling and gifting cash preserves the deduction.
